title: Of the inconvenience of greatness
paragraphs: Since we cannot reach it, let us revenge ourselves by railing at it; and yet it is not pure railing against anything to point out its defects, because in everything there are some to be found, however beautiful or however coveted. Greatness has, in general, this clear advantage, that it can lower itself when it pleases, and has, very nearly, the choice of both conditions; for a man does not fall from every height — there are several from which one can step down without falling. It does seem to me, though, that we rate it too high, and also overrate the resolve of those we have seen or heard of having despised it, or stepped down from it of their own accord; its essence is not so obviously useful that a man cannot, without a miracle, refuse it. I find it very hard to put up with misfortune; but to be content with a moderate measure of fortune, and to avoid greatness, I think a very easy matter. It is, to my mind, a virtue that I, who am no magician, could reach without any great effort. What, then, is to be expected of those who would still factor in the glory attached to refusing it — in which there may lurk worse ambition than even in the desire for greatness itself, and in the enjoyment of it? For ambition never behaves more truly to itself than when it proceeds by obscure and unfrequented routes.

I spur my courage to patience, but I rein it in as much as I can on the side of desire. I have as much to wish for as anyone, and I allow my wishes as much liberty and indiscretion; but even so it has never happened to me to wish for empire, or royalty, or the eminence of those high commanding fortunes; I do not aim that way; I love myself too well. When I do think of growing greater, it is only very moderately, and by a forced and timid advancement — such as is right for me in resolution, in prudence, in health, in beauty, and even in riches; but this supreme reputation, this mighty authority, weigh on my imagination; and, quite the opposite of the other, I should perhaps rather choose to be second or third in Périgord than first in Paris — at least, not lying about it, rather third in Paris than first. I would neither dispute with a porter, a wretched nobody, nor have crowds part in worship as I pass. I am brought up to a moderate condition, both by my own choice and by fortune; and I have shown, throughout the conduct of my life and projects, that I have rather avoided than otherwise the climbing above the rank where God has placed me by my birth: every natural lot is equally just and easy. My soul is such a poltroon that I measure good fortune not by its height, but by its ease.

But if my heart is not great enough, it is open enough to make up for it, by frankly laying bare its weakness at anyone's request. Suppose someone asked me to compare the life of L. Thorius Balbus, a brave man, handsome, learned, healthy, intelligent, abounding in every kind of comfort and pleasure, leading a quiet life entirely his own, his mind well prepared against death, superstition, pain, and the other troubles of human existence, dying at last in battle, sword in hand, for the defence of his country — on the one side; and on the other, the life of M. Regulus, so great and lofty as everyone knows, and his end admirable: the one without name and without dignity, the other exemplary and gloriously remembered. I would say, doubtless, as Cicero did, if only I could speak as well as he.
[Cicero, De Finibus, ii. 20, gives the preference to Regulus, and proclaims him the happier man.]

But if I were to compare them with my own, I should then also say that the first is as much within my reach, and within the desire I shape to my reach, as the second is far beyond it; the second I could only approach with reverence, the first I could readily attain by habit.

Let us return to our temporal greatness, from which we have wandered. I find every kind of mastery distasteful, whether to wield it or to submit to it. Otanes, one of the seven who had the right to claim the kingdom of Persia, did what I would happily have done: he gave up to his rivals his right of being raised to it, whether by election or by lot, on condition that he and his might live in the empire free from all authority and subjection — those of the ancient laws excepted — and might enjoy all the liberty that was not prejudicial to these, being as impatient of commanding as of being commanded.

The most difficult and demanding office in the world, in my view, is to discharge worthily that of a king. I excuse more of their mistakes than people commonly do, in view of the intolerable weight of their function, which staggers me. It is hard to keep measure in so unmeasured a power; and yet, even for those who are not of the best disposition, it is a singular spur to virtue to be set in a place where you cannot do the least good without its being put on record, and where the smallest benefit reaches so many men, and where your skill in governing, like that of preachers, is addressed mainly to the people — no very strict judges, easy to deceive and easy to please. There are few things on which we can give a sincere judgment, because there are few in which we don't have some private interest. Superiority and inferiority, dominion and subjection, are bound up with a natural envy and rivalry, and must perpetually encroach upon one another. I believe neither side as to the rights of the other; let reason therefore, which is inflexible and free of passion, decide, when we can lay hold of it. It is not above a month since I read two Scottish authors arguing this question, of whom the one who stands for the people makes the king worse off than a carter, while the one who writes for monarchy puts him several degrees above God in power and sovereignty.

Now the drawback of greatness that I have come to remark on here, prompted by something that has lately put it into my head, is this: there is perhaps nothing more enjoyable in our dealings with other people than the trials we make against one another out of rivalry of honour and worth, whether in exercises of the body or of the mind — in which sovereign greatness can have no true share. In truth, I have often thought that, by sheer force of respect, people treat princes disdainfully and unjustly in this very point. For the thing that infinitely offended me as a child, that those who exercised with me held back from doing their best because they thought me unworthy of their full effort, is what we see happen to princes every day, with everyone finding himself unworthy to contend with them. If we notice they have the least desire to win, every one of us will make it his business to give it to them, and will rather betray his own glory than offend theirs, putting only as much force into the engagement as is needed to save their honour. What share then have they in the contest, where everyone is on their side? I imagine those paladins of old times turning up to jousts and battles with enchanted weapons and bodies. Brisson,
[Plutarch, On Satisfaction or Tranquillity of the Mind. But in his essay How a Man may Distinguish a Flatterer from a Friend, he calls him Chriso.]

running against Alexander, deliberately missed his blow and made a fault in his career; Alexander scolded him for it, but he ought to have had him whipped. Considering this, Carneades said that "the sons of princes learned nothing properly except to handle horses, because in all their other exercises everyone bends and yields to them; but a horse, who is neither a flatterer nor a courtier, throws the son of a king with no more ceremony than he would throw the son of a porter."

Homer felt obliged to allow that Venus, gentle and delicate goddess as she was, should be wounded at the battle of Troy, in order to credit her with courage and boldness — qualities that cannot possibly belong to those exempt from danger. The gods are made to grow angry, to fear, to run away, to be jealous, to grieve, to be carried away by passions, so as to honour them with the virtues that, among us, are built upon those very imperfections. Whoever has no share in the hazard and difficulty can claim no share in the honour and pleasure that follow risky actions. It is a pity that a man should be so powerful that everything must give way to him; fortune in that case sets you too far apart from human company, and places you in too great a solitude. This easy, cheap knack of making everything bow under you is the enemy of every kind of pleasure: it is to slide, not to walk; to sleep, not to live. Imagine a man dressed in omnipotence: you overwhelm him; he has to beg disturbance and resistance as alms; his being and his good are in poverty. Evil to man is in its turn good, and good evil. Pain is not always to be avoided, nor pleasure always to be pursued.

Their good qualities are dead and lost, for they can only be perceived by comparison, and we put them out of reach of any: they have little knowledge of true praise, since their ears are deafened by such continual and uniform approval. Have they to do with the stupidest of all their subjects? They have no way to get any advantage of him; if he only says, "It is because he is my king," he thinks he has said enough to explain why he let himself be beaten. This quality stifles and consumes the other true and essential qualities: they are swallowed up in the royalty, which leaves them nothing to commend themselves with except actions that directly concern and serve the function of their place; it is so much to be a king that nothing else remains to them. The outer glare that surrounds him hides and shrouds him from us; our sight is turned back and dissipated by it, filled up and stopped by this overpowering light. The senate awarded the prize of eloquence to Tiberius; he refused it, judging that even if it had been deserved, he could draw no advantage from a verdict so partial, and so little free to judge.

Just as we give them every advantage of honour, so do we soothe and authorise all their vices and defects, not only by approval but also by imitation. Each of Alexander's followers carried his head on one side, as he did; and the flatterers of Dionysius would run into one another in his presence, and trip over and knock down whatever was underfoot, to show that they were as short-sighted as he. A hernia has even served to recommend a man for favour; I have seen deafness affected; and because the master hated his wife, Plutarch has seen his courtiers repudiate theirs, whom they loved; and, more than that, uncleanness and every kind of dissoluteness have come into fashion; as also disloyalty, blasphemy, cruelty, heresy, superstition, irreligion, effeminacy, and worse, if worse there be; by an example even more dangerous than that of Mithridates' flatterers, who, since their master claimed the honour of being a good physician, came to him to have incisions and cauteries made in their limbs — for the others let the soul, a more delicate and noble part, be cauterised.

But to end where I began: the Emperor Hadrian, debating with the philosopher Favorinus over the interpretation of some word, Favorinus quickly conceded him the victory; for which his friends rebuked him. "You talk simply," he said; "would you have me deny that he is wiser than I, who commands thirty legions?" Augustus wrote verses against Asinius Pollio, and "I," said Pollio, "keep quiet, for it is not prudence to write in contest with a man who has the power to proscribe." And they were right. For Dionysius, because he could not equal Philoxenus in poetry or Plato in philosophy, condemned the one to the quarries, and sent the other to be sold as a slave on the island of Aegina.
